title: Mohnish Pabrai's Interview at My First Million Podcast on April 4, 2024
summary: A wide-ranging podcast conversation on the link between entrepreneurship and investing, Buffett's early businesses, how Pabrai built his IT firm and then Pabrai Investment Funds, and his friendships with Buffett and Munger. Main takeaways: entrepreneurs and value investors use the same risk-minimizing brain (low risk, high return); the needle-moving decisions are the ones you never sell (Buffett's 12 bets, Nick Sleep, Reysas); look for mispricings where things are hated and unloved (IPSCO, coal, Turkey); most people should index; and be a harsh grader of the people you let into your life.

ideas.idea: Investing and entrepreneurship use the same part of the brain, and investing lets you spend 80% of your time on the strategy work that is only 3-5% of running a business.
ideas.detail: Buffett says he is a better investor because he is a businessman and vice versa. In a business, 3-5% of time goes to figuring out strategy and 95-97% to blocking and tackling; in investing you do not need a Danley to fix the pinball machines, so that 3% becomes 80%. Pabrai finds it strange to meet investors who have never been entrepreneurs.

ideas.idea: The brain specializes in the window from about age 11 to 20, so the calling you start in that decade gives you an expertise nobody starting at 20 can match even at 50.
ideas.detail: Michelangelo, Bill Gates and Buffett all started specializing at 10 or 11; Buffett ran Stable Boy Selections, the Wilson Coin Operated Amusement pinball business in 40 barbershops and a Rolls Royce rental, and had $15,000 (about $150,000 today) by age 17. Parents' biggest responsibility is exposing kids to what they think their passion is in that window.

ideas.idea: When judging a CEO, find out whether they ran a lemonade stand at 12, because if they did not they will not be that great at business at 30.
ideas.detail: Pabrai's own teen years sitting on his father's board at 10-11, running the gold jewelry business in Dubai and shadowing sales calls at 15 gave him an edge over engineers and marketers with 20 more years of experience. He says he had finished many MBAs by age 16.

ideas.idea: See's Candies taught Buffett and Munger the power of brands and pricing power, and without See's they would never have bought Coke.
ideas.detail: Buffett raised See's prices every December 26th by 10-15% when inflation was 3% and volumes still rose; they paid $25 million (three times book value) and could have paid $200 million; billions in dividends have flowed to Berkshire over 50 years. That lesson led to putting a quarter of Berkshire's book value into Coke in 1988. Unlike See's, which did not travel outside California, Coke is ubiquitous and has no aftertaste.

ideas.idea: Entrepreneurs do not take risks; they do everything in their power to minimize risk, which is exactly what value investors do: low risk, high return.
ideas.detail: Buffett's pinball business risked $15 per machine plus $3 in parts, with each new machine bought only from cash the previous one produced. Venture-backed businesses are under 0.1% of the million businesses formed each year in the US and are a different high-risk animal because the VC only needs one of ten bets to work. Pabrai started his own firm with $30,000 from his 401k and $70,000 of credit card limits while keeping his job for nine months, doing just enough not to get fired.

ideas.idea: If you can start an airline with no money, you can start any business with no money; you replace capital with creative thinking.
ideas.detail: Richard Branson got Virgin Atlantic off the ground with zero equity by persistently calling Boeing to lease an idle 747 at $200-300k a month in arrears, collecting ticket revenue two or three months before flights and paying for fuel 30 days after landing, giving negative working capital.

ideas.idea: The Patels came to own 70% of US motels by being the lowest-cost producer, and Munger told his friends never to compete with a Patel.
ideas.detail: Refugees expelled from Uganda by Idi Amin in the early 1970s bought 10-14 room motels, lived in two rooms, fired the staff, did all the work themselves and undercut neighbors' rates while running 100% occupancy, then financed nephews to repeat it for 50 years. Munger said if you find yourself competing with a Patel, find another game to play.

ideas.idea: An idea is worthless; execution is what has value, so you do not need patents and can tell competitors your trade secrets without them changing behavior.
ideas.detail: Pabrai took the $1 million he received in the mid-1990s from selling part of his IT business and compounded it to $13 million from 1995 to 2005 (about 70% a year) while running the company part-time, which convinced him to switch to investing full-time.

ideas.idea: Pabrai Investment Funds was structured like the Buffett partnerships: no management fee, first 6% to investors, then one-fourth to the manager above that.
ideas.detail: A 2-and-20 hedge fund on $1 billion takes $20 million for breathing plus $20 million on a 10% year, leaving investors with 6%; under the Buffett structure the manager takes $10 million and only when performance is earned. Started in 1999 as a hobby with $1 million from eight friends, the fund reached $600 million in 2007 after roughly mid-30s% annual returns with no down years.

ideas.idea: If you beat the market, investors will swim through shark-infested waters to find you, so fundraising is really about performance plus enlisting existing investors to spread the word.
ideas.detail: Because SEC rules bar soliciting the public, Pabrai told investors at annual meetings that their sole purpose on earth was to bring assets to Pabrai Investment Funds. Investors went from 8 to 17 to 25 in two years and assets from $1 million to $2.5 million to $10 million.

ideas.idea: In 1999 Pabrai did a 180 from tech to classic Ben Graham deep value, buying funeral homes at two times earnings and steel companies at three times earnings while the dot-com bubble inflated.
ideas.detail: People counted eyeballs instead of earnings; Pets.com had multi-billion valuations with no revenue. The day the NASDAQ peaked around March 8-9, 2000 was the day Berkshire hit a multi-year low; NASDAQ fell from 5,000 to about 1,200, a 75% drop, while Pabrai was the only guy making money for his investors.

ideas.idea: Be a harsh grader of people: bring the three or four exceptional ones into your inner circle, exclude the bad ones, and treat the 92 you cannot figure out the same as the useless ones.
ideas.detail: Buffett told Pabrai at the 2007 charity lunch (won for $650,000, though he was willing to pay $2 million as a tuition bill) that in a party of 100 he could only identify 3-4 exceptional and 3-4 bad people; there is a gravitational pull toward the people you hang out with and loyalty should not keep substandard people in your life. With infinite humans there is no penalty for excluding a good one you cannot figure out, but a big drain from including a bad one. Pabrai shortcut this by making Munger's friends his friends since Munger had done the filtering.

ideas.idea: Seek out givers, avoid takers, and above all be a giver, because when you are a giver the universe conspires to help you.
ideas.detail: From Adam Grant's Give and Take: takers extract, matchers keep score in their heads and end up losing, givers help selflessly. Buffett and Munger are great examples of givers; the best way to get the most is not to ask for anything.

ideas.idea: Heads I win, tails I do not lose much: look for bets where the odds are heavily in your favor, and auction-driven public markets keep serving up such anomalies in hated and unloved areas.
ideas.detail: IPSCO in 2003-04 traded at $45 with $15 a share of cash, no debt and contracted earnings of $15 a share for each of the next two years, so the plant came free; Pabrai put 10% of assets in, and a Swedish company bought it at $160. In 2023 he spent seven or eight months on coal, where a business that would produce about $1 billion a year of cash for 50 years could be bought for under $2 billion. The 'Trouble is opportunity' sign in his office is a John Templeton quote copied from Prem Watsa's desk: be greedy when the world is fearful, and when the world runs away from coal, run toward it; endowments barred from coal are why it gets mispriced.

ideas.idea: Public markets are more irrational than private ones because a stock's 52-week range is often 70 to 130 while the underlying business changes little, so an investor only needs to be patient and make two good investments a year.
ideas.detail: If his house were listed on the NYSE its quote would wiggle 20-30% above and below its worth, whereas a realtor would say it is worth $2 million day after day; you cannot buy a whole IPSCO at the stock price because an intelligent seller faces an intelligent buyer.

ideas.idea: More than 99% of people are best off buying a low-cost index fund; only the sliver who can value businesses, buy well below worth and hold patiently should invest actively.
ideas.detail: The index is too dumb to know it owns NVIDIA and even dumber in that it never sells; it held Apple for 10 years. Frictional costs of an ETF are single-digit basis points. Taking stock tips from a guy on TV is a big red flag because he will not be there when it is down 30%.

ideas.idea: Patience is the number one trait of a great investor; if you love watching paint dry you will do very well.
ideas.detail: He cites Elaine's boyfriend on Seinfeld who stares at the seat back for a whole flight, and Pascal's line that all man's miseries stem from his inability to sit quietly in a room alone.

ideas.idea: Compounding has three variables (starting capital, rate of return, length of runway) and the rule of 72 should be taught in high school so people start the engine early.
ideas.detail: $10,000 saved at 22 in an index at 10% doubles every seven years, six doubles by 64, so 2^6 = 64 times, or $640,000, and every later year's savings compounds the same way; that is why a janitor can leave $4 million to a college. Buffett has an 87-year runway. Pabrai's own plan was 15% of salary plus a 2% match into a 401k; let it be a boring Vanguard index and the tortoise wins.

ideas.idea: Circle the wagons: Buffett's 2023 letter says only 12 decisions in 58 years moved the needle, and the key to those was not the buy decision but never selling.
ideas.detail: Berkshire compounded 20%+ for 58 years, roughly 16 doubles or 64,000x; out of at least 400 decisions 12 mattered, a 4% hit rate for the God of investing, so mortals will have 2% but only need to get rich once. See's has been held 50 years, Coke 40-plus. When you own a small piece of a great business, find something else to do with your time, like bridge or golf.

ideas.idea: Ajit Jain is the best investment Berkshire ever made, and his discipline of passing on inadequately priced super-cat insurance and writing big only when premiums are rich is the no-called-strikes principle applied to insurance.
ideas.detail: Munger said the search fee to hire Ajit in 1985-86 was Berkshire's best investment; the business he built is worth north of $100 billion. In 2023 Ajit wrote Florida hurricane reinsurance with a $15 billion max payout for about $5 billion of premium and paid out perhaps $300-400 million; in most years the premium offered was $2 billion and he passed. After the Baltimore ship loss of $3-5 billion, Berkshire will likely write marine cover when everyone else refuses.

ideas.idea: Bitcoin is outside his circle of competence and, if forced to guess, he thinks it will end badly because it has no intrinsic value; most people should take a pass.
ideas.detail: The dollar at least has the full faith and credit of the US government backed by the American people; most Bitcoin holders cannot say what it should be worth or why. Tesla likewise goes in the too-hard pile even though he calls Elon Musk an exceptional capital allocator and hirer.

ideas.idea: Nick Sleep found Amazon by reading annual reports until he was blue in the face, then held it as it grew to 80% of his money, showing that once you have a great business you should leave it alone.
ideas.detail: Amazon looked expensive on a PE basis because growth capex was expensed, but Bezos's letters showed very high returns on capital and low-risk bets like AWS (worked) and Fire (did not). When the UK regulator pressured them, Nick and Zach returned capital and Nick put one-third each into Berkshire, Amazon and Costco; even after sloppily halving Amazon at 80% it went very well. The Walton family similarly keeps nearly all their net worth in Walmart stock they do not run and sleeps fine.

ideas.idea: Reysas in Turkey traded at 2% of liquidation value in 2019; Pabrai bought a third of the company for $8 million and treats it the way the Waltons treat Walmart, ignoring the stock price as long as the father and son keep running it well.
ideas.detail: Turkey's largest warehouse operator had 12 million square feet at $70-80 a square foot, about $1 billion of property against $200 million of debt, and a $16 million market cap; warehouses are 99% leased, inflation indexed, to Amazon, Ikea, Carrefour, Mercedes and Toyota. Four years later market cap is about $500 million, up nearly 30x in dollars despite the lira going from 5 to 33 per dollar, and the business may be worth $1.5-2 billion. The key to moving the needle is inactivity.

ideas.idea: It is the norm that great businesses are sloppy with execution, so Zuckerberg's 180 from spendthrift to Patel at Meta made an already great business an excellent capital allocator.
ideas.detail: Meta was a country club with spending in every area; he tightened it up and it showed in the numbers. It is very rare to find a great business that is also tight-fisted.

ideas.idea: Charlie Munger's epitaph, 'I tried to be useful,' captures him: he selflessly gave partners the better deal, transformed every institution he touched, never complained, and extracted everything from his mind and body to the end.
ideas.detail: Without Munger there is no Berkshire. He was arranging a non-profit grant the day before he died and bought a stock six days before. When facing blindness in his remaining eye a decade ago he simply said he would have to learn braille; Pabrai twice took personal problems to him and doing exactly what Charlie said made them disappear.
